source: Simpson, Kozak, Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation
finding: Frontier models do well on flat multi-route rules but fail on rules with nested UNLESS-UNLESS exception chains. In March 2026 the failures were systematic, not random.
numbers: English-language section: 43/43 (100%) for top models. Spacecraft section (3-level exception chain), 68 scenarios: Claude Opus 4.6 61/68 (89.7%, Wilson CI 80.2-94.9). 10 reruns on each of the 7 failing scenarios = 70 trials, 0 correct (one-sided upper bound 4.19% per trial). Cheaper models lower: 51/68 (75.0%) and 22/48 (45.8%) in the table.
quote: A is required UNLESS B applies, UNLESS C overrides B
limits: Vendor paper (Aethis) selling an SMT engine; the benchmark is the authors' own. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Nested exceptions are a known weak point. A scaffold should expand each exception level as its own explicit step instead of trusting one pass.

source: Simpson et al. (2026) Exception Chain Collapse, silent drift and v3.8 replication
finding: The same model alias changed accuracy between March and April 2026 with no version bump. Several failure cells closed, and one earlier claim was withdrawn.
numbers: Opus 4.6 spacecraft 89.7% (March) -> 98.5% (April). GPT-5.4 construction insurance 96.6% -> 100% (74/74). The v3.6/v3.7 claim GPT-5.4 low reasoning 7/11 (63.6%) was withdrawn after an instrumented replication gave 11/11. GPT-5.3 stayed at 7/11 (63.6%, CI 35.4-84.8); an earlier 27% figure was a configuration error. GPT-5-nano 62/68 -> 60/68.
limits: Small N per cell (11 to 68). Authors flag their own earlier errors.
agent_relevance: Every number for a model on defeasible tasks is a dated snapshot. Re-run tests at time of use; do not bake model-specific tuning into the schema.

source: Simpson et al. (2026) Exception Chain Collapse, section 6.7 enhanced prompt test
finding: A prompt telling the model to evaluate each exemption independently cut missed cases but caused new over-application. Net accuracy fell.
numbers: Enhanced prompt net accuracy 64.7% (CI 52.8-75.0) versus 89.7% baseline. False negatives 7 -> 4 but 20 new false positives. Re-run gave the same 20 FP / 4 FN with different scenarios failing. Baseline failures were identical across runs (the same 7).
limits: One enhanced prompt variant, one main model (Opus 4.6); GPT-5.4 showed 1 extra failure. A three-variant preregistered comparison (few-shot, self-critique, decomposition) is described separately and not used here.
agent_relevance: A general 'be careful with exceptions' instruction is not a safe fix. Check error in both directions, not only recall of exceptions.

source: Simpson et al. (2026) Exception Chain Collapse, section 6.10 LegalBench external validation
finding: On 9 LegalBench tasks (949 held-out cases) a rule engine built from LLM-authored rules beat three frontier LLMs. The margin was largest on multi-prong rule application.
numbers: Paired test discordant cases (engine only correct / LLM only correct): vs Sonnet 4.6 44/15, vs Opus 4.7 34/13 (p=0.003), vs GPT-5.4 340/35. Combined p at most 0.003 for each. Up to +41 percentage points over the Anthropic models on curated multi-prong tasks. GPT-5.4 on multi-prong tasks: hearsay 85.1%, personal_jurisdiction 96.0%, jcrew_blocker 92.6%.
limits: Three tasks were hand-curated and hint iteration used the test split before preregistration (authors flag this). 27 per-task tests without full correction. Table text was garbled in extraction, so the p-to-row mapping is partly inferred.
agent_relevance: Supports a hybrid loop: model writes the rule set, a deterministic checker runs it. Fits a verify-with-code operator.

source: Simpson et al. (2026) Exception Chain Collapse, section 6.10.4 prompt-format sensitivity
finding: GPT-5.4 collapsed to a yes-bias under the LegalBench few-shot format. Dropping the few-shot examples fixed most of it.
numbers: cuad_covenant_not_to_sue: 83/154 (53.9%) few-shot, yes-rate 98.7% (yes on 304/308); zero-shot 143/154 (92.9%), a +39 point recovery, yes-rate 45.5%. Engine still higher at 150/154 (97.4%), McNemar b=7, c=0, p=0.016. Four other tasks GPT-5.4 36.4% to 66.9% while Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 cleared 87% on all five.
limits: Zero-shot rerun shown for one task only. Authors say this is format-coupled, not a capability ceiling.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples can skew the label prior. Check the label balance of outputs as a cheap sanity test in any classifying step.

source: Steging, Renooij, Verheij (2025) Parameterized Argumentation-based Reasoning Tasks for Benchmarking Generative Language Models (ICAIL 2025)
finding: Witness-testimony puzzles built from argument attack graphs. Models fail even at low complexity and are inconsistent.
numbers: Linear graphs, 1-25 arguments, 100 variants each (2,500 prompts). Accuracy: GPT-4o-mini 54.38, GPT-4o 72.31, Gemini-1.5-flash 64.64, Gemini-1.5-pro 60.32, Claude-3.5-haiku 58.84, Claude-3.5-sonnet 77.32. o1-preview 100.0 on 75 prompts. GPT-4o with up to 50 arguments: 63.05. Baseline about 50.
limits: Short paper, older non-reasoning models. o1-preview only 75 prompts. Class balance is skewed, so the authors add MCC.
agent_relevance: A plain attack chain is easy to state and still breaks non-reasoning models. Use a reasoning model or an explicit in/out/undecided labelling step.

source: Steging et al. (2025) parameterized benchmark, non-linear and shuffled graphs
finding: With branching attack graphs, accuracy looks high only because the answer is mostly 'no'. MCC and recall show weak reasoning. Even o1-preview errs.
numbers: Non-linear (2,540 prompts, up to 15 arguments; 'yes' correct in 8.85%). Accuracy / recall / MCC: GPT-4o-mini 74.57 / 18.81 / 21.08; GPT-4o 51.77 / 14.95 / 24.21; Claude-3.5-sonnet 86.81 / 38.15 / 48.73; Claude-3.5-haiku accuracy 33.6. Shuffled statement order: Claude-3.5-sonnet accuracy 89.72 but MCC 32.25 (down from 48.73). o1-preview on 262 hard prompts: accuracy 91.6, recall 35.29, precision 100, MCC 56.73.
limits: The hard subset was chosen from prompts that GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-sonnet got wrong (508 unique prompts), so it is adversarial. GPT-4o tends to follow the longest path and ignore the other attacker.
agent_relevance: Order of statements changes results, so the scaffold should restate attacks in a fixed normal form. Report MCC or recall when positives are rare.

source: Steging et al. (2025) parameterized benchmark, parity pattern and chain length
finding: In a linear chain the answer depends only on parity of the chain length. Most models did better on odd lengths and drifted toward the 50% baseline as chains grew.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-flash and Gemini-pro approach the 50% baseline at larger numbers of arguments. o1-preview noticed the odd-even pattern in some answers and scored 100% on 75 prompts.
limits: Curves are in figures; per-length numbers are not in the text.
agent_relevance: Attack on an attacker (reinstatement) is the same pattern that humans find hard in the angle A studies; models show it too.

source: Allaway & McKeown (2024) Evaluating Defeasible Reasoning in LLMs with DEFREASING
url: local PDF read in D:/research_scratch/E11.06/defreasing.pdf (arXiv id not verified)
finding: 95k questions on property inheritance with generics (exceptions allowed). No model is good across all five reasoning patterns.
numbers: 12 instruction-tuned LLMs; best models reach only 0.64 overall macro-F1. A model can score near 100% on one pattern and near 0 on another. Dataset label alignment with human annotators 79% on one subset (annotator agreement 40-50% on some types) and 96% on others.
limits: Built from generic semantics and earlier human data, so labels on some categories are contested. Generics, not statutes.
agent_relevance: Even the simple does-the-subtype-inherit step is unstable. Add a check asking what extra information would strengthen or weaken the conclusion.

source: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: 28 LLMs on 20 default-reasoning patterns. Chain-of-thought often hurt. Many models treat 'Birds fly' as 'all birds fly'.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy at temp 0: Claude 3 Opus 96.51, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96.01, GPT-4 (0613) 93.52, Claude 3 Sonnet 91.36, GPT-4o (2024-08-06) 89.03, Gemini 1.5 Pro 83.55, GPT-3.5 (0125) 48.00. CoT delta: Claude 3 Sonnet -16.28, GPT-4 (0613) -12.62, Gemini 1.5 Flash -18.77, Llama 2 Chat 70B -41.52, GPT-4o (2024-05-13) +17.44, GPT-4o (2024-08-06) +4.98. Mean CoT drop -11.14 (SD 15.74) among models above 75% zero-shot.
limits: Zero-shot CoT only, pre-2025 models. Wording variants of one pattern correlated from 0.99 down to -0.05, so single-prompt results are fragile.
agent_relevance: Do not assume step-by-step text helps on default rules. Test each scaffold step against a plain answer, and keep the exception-versus-universal distinction explicit in the written state.

source: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025) Generics, few-shot effects and error patterns
finding: Few-shot helps weak models and not strong ones. A main error under CoT is treating a generic as a universal.
numbers: Few-shot delta: Claude 3 Haiku +25.08, Llama 2 Chat 7B +28.74, GPT-4o (2024-05-13) +16.27, Mixtral +16.11; Claude 3 Opus -6.81, Llama 3.1 8B -10.29. Wording-variant correlations 0.99, 0.99, 0.88, 0.54, 0.43, 0.47, -0.05.
limits: Error taxonomy built by manual inspection of three models only.
agent_relevance: Summarising a rule as a universal is a known failure. The state should keep 'normally' and 'unless' wording.

source: Tachmazidis, Batsakis, Antoniou (2024) Benchmarking Defeasible Reasoning with LLMs - Initial Experiments
finding: A defeasible-logic reasoner benchmark was put into text and run on GPT-4o on 8 theories in 4 settings. The model mishandled conflicts without priorities, and statement order mattered.
numbers: 8 theories x 4 settings (random or sequential order, conclusion true or false). All four settings correct for chain(8), chains(8), circle(8), circles(8), hierarchies(2,4). levels-(5) wrong in all 4; levels(5) wrong in 2 of 4; dag(3,2) wrong in 1 of 4 (a hallucinated entity swap).
limits: Tiny qualitative study: one run per cell (32 cells), one model.
agent_relevance: Where rules conflict and no priority is given the model invents a resolution. The agent should mark 'no priority given' as undecided.

source: Antoniou & Batsakis (2023) Defeasible Reasoning with Large Language Models - Initial Experiments
finding: ChatGPT answered simple rule-and-exception cases correctly but disregarded specificity (the more specific rule wins) until told.
numbers: A handful of hand-built examples (including a Privacy Act style case); Table 1 compares ChatGPT answers with defeasible-logic answers. After a prompt naming specificity it applied it correctly in the example discussed.
limits: A few hand-picked cases, no trial counts, one chat model, informal.
agent_relevance: List specificity and recency priority rules explicitly in the schema; the model uses them once named.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: Natural Language Reasoning with Contradictory Information
finding: A defeasible benchmark with rules, conflicts and preferences between rules. Few-shot LLMs do poorly, and more conflict means worse results.
numbers: Depth 1-3 variants; 1,000 train / 500 val / 1,000 test per variant, balanced labels (majority baseline 33%). Models: BERT-large, T5 XXL, PaLM 62B and 540B few-shot with CoT, FLAN-PaLM 540B, prompt-tuned PaLM 62B. Accuracy fell monotonically as conflict probability rose (0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8); BERT near random at medium and high conflict. PaLM 540B better than 62B.
limits: Exact accuracies are only in figures, so no table numbers recorded. 2023 models, synthetic text.
agent_relevance: Conflict resolution by preference does not come free from pretraining. The agent should state which source or rule wins and why before using a conclusion.

source: Freedman, Dejl, Gorur, Yin, Rago, Toni (2025) Argumentative LLMs for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: An LLM writes a pro and a con argument per claim, scores each, and a formal semantics (DF-QuAD) computes the verdict. Accuracy is about the same as chain-of-thought.
numbers: Datasets TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim; models include Mistral-7B, Mixtral, Llama 3 8B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4o. StrategyClaim with Llama 3 8B: Direct 0.77, CoT 0.76, ArgLLM depth-1 with estimated base score 0.81 (depth-2: 0.78). Authors' own summary: ArgLLMs perform comparably with CoT.
limits: Prompts chosen on 200-sample pilot sets with two models. Gains are in contestability and faithful explanation, not accuracy. Depth-2 trees did not help.
agent_relevance: Shows an attack and support graph can sit inside a loop at no accuracy cost, with a traceable verdict. Candidate for an explicit-attacks operator.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying
finding: A four-stage pipeline has the model answer eight critical questions drawn from Toulmin (data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal) about its own reasoning before the final answer. Judge scores improve.
numbers: MT-Bench reasoning and math, five models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5-pro-001, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Llama 3.1-70b, Nemotron-51b). Judge GPT-4o, scale 1-10. Average gain over baseline and CoT +4.61% on reasoning and +5.4% on math. CQoT best or joint best in 19 of 20 comparisons. Llama 3.1-70b with CQoT beat baseline GPT-4o on reasoning.
limits: LLM judge from one of the tested families; small benchmark; Nemotron-51b did worse than CoT on reasoning (authors guess a 70B size threshold). Not tested on legal tasks.
agent_relevance: Closest published case of Toulmin used as a check inside an LLM loop. A critical-question gate is cheap to add before the final answer.

source: Gupta, Zuckerman, O'Connor (2024) Harnessing Toulmin's theory for zero-shot argument explication (ACL 2024)
finding: Naming the theory in the prompt makes models split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant and state the missing warrant.
numbers: Success rate (responses with all three Toulmin terms), ARCT: 99.0, 94.6, 75.2, 35.0 and MCT: 100.0, 95.4, 90.2, 42.5 for GPT-4, GPT-3, Llama-2-70B, Falcon-40B in that order (column order inferred from the text). Human check of 150 pairs (300 judgments per type): warrant acceptable for gold 45.7%, GPT-4 61.7%, Llama-2-70B 26.3%. Kappa 0.24 and 0.31 for model warrants.
limits: Model-column order is uncertain from PDF extraction. Agreement among raters is low. Tests argument explication, not rule application.
agent_relevance: Toulmin's warrant and rebuttal slots can be elicited cheaply. Implicit warrants are where hidden exceptions live, so the schema can ask for them.

source: Bex & Prakken (2026) Toulmin Argumentation Logic (COMMA 2026)
finding: Gives Toulmin's scheme a formal logic (TAL) with a proved correspondence to ASPIC+, so rebuttals and qualifiers have a defined attack and acceptability. The authors say it can serve as an evaluation standard and prompting basis for LLM arguments.
numbers: No experiments. Cites three LLM-Toulmin works: Castagna et al. 2024, Gupta et al. 2024, Park et al. 2025 (Korean criminal counterarguments).
quote: can serve both as an evaluation standard for LLM-generated arguments
limits: Theory only; proposes, does not test.
agent_relevance: Supplies a formal checklist of legitimate attacks (rebut, undercut, undermine) for the agent's self-critique.

source: Calegari & Sartor (2020) Burden of Persuasion in Argumentation
finding: A two-stage labelling: first accept, reject or undecided; then the allocated burden of persuasion settles the undecided cases. Also handles inversion of the burden for sub-arguments.
numbers: Formal paper, no data.
limits: No LLM test of burden-of-persuasion prompting was found in this pass.
agent_relevance: A tie-break rule for deadlock: when for and against stay undecided, the side that carries the burden loses.

source: Horner, Mateis, Governatori, Ciabattoni (2025) Toward Robust Legal Text Formalization into Defeasible Deontic Logic using LLMs
finding: LLMs turn legal norms into defeasible deontic rules; a two-stage pipeline with a refinement step improves recall and consistency. A prior paper's metrics were recomputed and found overstated.
numbers: Australian Telecommunications Consumer Protections Code. Term-identification F1: GPT-4.1 simple chain 0.74, DeepSeek-R1 0.79, DeepSeek-R1 single interaction 0.80, DeepSeek-R1 with Claude Sonnet 4 refinement 0.82. Prior paper claimed F1 86.74%; recomputed 79.03% (49/65 = 75.38% recall, not 90.78%).
limits: One legal code; small gold set (about 65-70 atoms); results vary by model and step.
agent_relevance: A model-writes-rules, checker-runs-rules loop is feasible, but rule drafting is the weak link at about 0.8 F1.

source: Mishra et al. (2025) Investigating the Shortcomings of LLMs in Step-by-Step Legal Reasoning
finding: On Civil Procedure multiple choice, correct final answers often rest on flawed steps. Feeding an error taxonomy back into prompts adds only a little.
numbers: Accuracy-to-correctness drop averaged 27% across LLMs (31.4% for Llama-3-8B-Instruct). GPT-4o had 78.4% of premises error-free. 96% of chains from false premises had a misinterpretation error. Auto-evaluator recall 86.17-93.85%. Taxonomy feedback gave up to 4% accuracy gain; for Gemini-1.5-Flash it helped only CoT and Plan-and-Solve.
limits: Civil procedure includes analogical reasoning, not only defeasible rules. Auto-evaluator agreement with humans 78.1%.
agent_relevance: A right answer is not enough. The schema should score the chain, not only the final choice.

source: Nananukul et al. (2025) LOGicalThought: Logic-Based Ontological Grounding of LLMs for High-Assurance Reasoning
finding: An LLM extracts a symbolic graph and a defeasible logic program (ErgoAI) from the guidelines, then answers with both as context. Helps weak models most.
numbers: Four benchmarks (ContractNLI, SARA, BiomedNLI, Dungeons and Dragons), six LLMs. +11.84% over all baselines on average, +4.41% over the best baseline. Up to +5.5% defeasible, +10.2% negation, +13.2% implication versus the strongest baseline. Mistral-7B 45.2 -> 53.4 and LLaMA-8B 44.3 -> 50.4 on ContractNLI. Small drops: -0.8% ContractNLI defeasible, -3.2% SARA negation. Reasoning steps +21.5% versus CoT; false-negative reasoning cases 41% (CoT) -> 28%.
limits: Part of the benchmark was rewritten by GPT-4o with a sample audit. Defeasible gains are the smallest of the three modes.
agent_relevance: An explicit exceptions list as extra context gives a modest gain; extracting the rules becomes the new failure point.

source: Li, Fang, Chen, Li, Liao (2025) Enhancing Conflict Resolution in Language Models via Abstract Argumentation
finding: Fine-tuning on abstract argumentation frameworks with step-by-step acceptability explanations beats zero-shot CoT and generalizes better than answer-only training.
numbers: Zero-shot baselines (conflict-free proportion / at-least-one-valid extension, complete semantics): Qwen2.5-7B 0.71 / 0.62, Llama3-8B 0.51 / 0.42. After SFT: Qwen2.5-SFT 1.00 / 0.99 (com), Llama3-SFT 1.00 / 0.99 (com) and 1.00 / 0.86 (prf). Without explanations accuracy fell as low as 30% on frameworks above 25 arguments.
limits: Needs training; abstract frameworks, not legal text; generalization tested only to larger frameworks of the same kind.
agent_relevance: Training is out of scope for us, but it shows an in-context version needs a written step trace for each acceptance step.

source: Cooper, Sadhu, Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
finding: A dataset where the model proposes an exception that fixes a default theory and keeps other conclusions. Simple symbolic repair solves all released tasks, so the panel mostly measures format.
numbers: Release 1.0.0: 225,507 records over 2,099 source families; evaluation panel 336 tasks, two prompt styles. Success direct/structured: GPT-5.6 Sol 336/336, GPT-6.1 Sol 336/336, Claude Sonnet 5 306/244, Claude Sonnet 5.5 133/336, DeepSeek-V4-Pro 273/38, Kimi-K2.6 205/99. Four deployments had 1,054 failures: 652 contract violations, 366 token-limit cuts, 36 semantic misses. No collateral loss on admissible L3 edits.
limits: Training and revision studies are planned, not run. Prompt style swings one model from 133 to 336. The authors call generic repair a shortcut.
agent_relevance: Output format and token budget cause more failures than logic. Structured-output prompts must be tested per model.

source: Batzoglou (2026) ABD: Default-Exception Abduction in Finite First-Order Worlds
finding: A solver-checked benchmark where the model writes an exception rule that repairs a default theory. Validity saturates for strong models, but they over-generate exceptions.
numbers: Eleven frontier LLMs, 600 instances, three observation regimes (Full, Partial, Skeptical), seven default theories. Strongest high-validity models still carry 1 to 1.5 extra exceptions per world over the solver minimum. GPT-5.4 is a low-gap outlier with lower validity. On holdout worlds, Skeptical-regime rules often break.
limits: Finite toy worlds with first-order output; per-model validity percentages were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Models patch conflicts with broad exceptions. Prefer the smallest exception that fixes the case, and test that other conclusions stay unchanged.

source: Prajescu & Confalonieri (2025) Argumentation-Based Explainability for Legal AI
finding: A survey of argumentation-based explanation methods for legal AI against regulatory needs. Argues formal argument structures give contestable explanations.
numbers: No experiments with LLMs.
limits: Review only; no measured results.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the agent's reasoning trail should be an attack-and-defence graph a user can contest.

source: Scheffers (2026) Creating an argumentation-based system for fraud detection in law enforcement with LLM support (CEUR RELAF'26)
finding: A qualitative study of people building an ASPIC+-style fraud classification system with and without an LLM. The LLM was not useful for turning legal text into rules but helped people start.
numbers: Qualitative focus group, small N (not extracted). The LLM group started faster and felt less overwhelmed at first.
limits: Exploratory, ChatGPT in browser in Dec 2025, no accuracy measure.
agent_relevance: Text-to-argument-rule translation by LLM is unreliable, so keep a human or a test in that step.

source: LLM-ASPIC+ (IOS Press, FAIA 2025, doi 10.3233/FAIA250981), from search snippet only
finding: A search summary says it pairs an LLM with ASPIC+ and tests on BoardGameQA-style data and a new MineQA set.
numbers: Snippet only: 87.1% on BoardGameQA-2 and 82.6% on BoardGameQA-3 (not verified, not opened).
limits: Not opened. Authors and exact method unconfirmed. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, the closest published LLM + ASPIC+ loop; open it first in the next pass.

source: Park, Choi, Park (2025) Objection, your honour! LLM-driven approach for generating Korean criminal case counterarguments (AI and Law)
finding: Cited by Bex and Prakken as an LLM use of Toulmin's scheme for counterargument generation. Reference only.
numbers: No numbers; only the citation in the COMMA 2026 paper was read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a Toulmin-rebuttal prompt in a legal setting; open in the next pass.
